new_statements.quote: Der dynamische Akzent wird durch den Acutus ' ausgedrückt. Sehr häufig fällt er auf die drittletzte Silbe, weshalb in dem Falle von einer Bezeichnung des Akzents abgesehen ist. [...] Fällt der Akzent auf die erste Silbe eines zweisilbigen Wortes, so ist er ebenfalls nicht bezeichnet. Enklitische Worte sind durch — mit dem zugehörigen Worte verbunden, auf den sie den Akzent werfen. Manche Worte sind zweigipflich, doch ist eine besondere Bezeichnung für den zweiten Akzent nicht angewandt. Die Akzentuierung schwankt zuweilen bei denselben Worten.
new_statements.translation: The dynamic accent is expressed by the acute '. Very often it falls on the antepenultimate syllable, for which reason in that case the marking of the accent is dispensed with. [...] If the accent falls on the first syllable of a disyllabic word, it is likewise not marked. Enclitic words are joined by — to the word they belong to, onto which they throw the accent. Some words have two peaks, but no special marking for the second accent is used. The accentuation sometimes fluctuates in the same words.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's Gordon record (antepenultimate stress = antepenultimate) as the most frequent position, and adds that it is a tendency with fluctuation, enclitic shift and occasional double peaks. Preuss's material is from Jesús María and San Francisco (El Nayar), i.e. the catalog's variety.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (a dynamic, not pitch, accent) most often falls on the antepenultimate syllable; that is the unmarked default in Preuss's transcription (disyllables default to initial stress). Enclitics shift the accent onto the host word; the dictionary (line 46014ff.) marks the accent on headwords only where the word is independent or prefixes do not change it, again treating the antepenult as the usual place.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Manche Worte sind zweigipflich' — some words have two accent peaks, but Preuss does not mark the second one.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent is only 'very often' antepenultimate, not always; enclitics attract the accent; accentuation fluctuates between tokens of the same word; when the accent and the saltillo (glottal stop) fall on the same vowel, either half of the vowel may carry it.
new_statements.identity_note: Jáuregui 2025 (not opened) describes Tereseño (Santa Teresa) Cora, a different Cora variety from El Nayar Cora elna1235 (the prior pass's maps it to sant1424; unverified). Preuss 1912 covers Jesús María and San Francisco (El Nayar); Kim & Valdovinos 2014 cover Jesús María ('Mariteco') Cora only, two speakers, words in isolation.

new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog's fixed: antepenultimate syllable record in kind: it characterises Cora stress as lexical (roughly half of monomorphemic disyllables are final-stressed, which a fixed antepenult/leftward rule would not predict) rather than positionally fixed. The two are not strictly incompatible, since the catalog's pattern string only specifies 3+ syllable words and K&V only examined 1-2 syllable words, but K&V give no positional rule and use 'lexical stress' throughout. Variety: Jesús María (Mariteco), El Nayar, i.e. within elna1235.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mariteco (Jesús María) Cora has lexical stress, cued by high pitch on the stressed syllable and devoicing of final unstressed vowels; monomorphemic disyllables are stressed either initially or finally (24+4 initial vs 22 final for one speaker, 25+5 initial vs 37 final for the other, table (12) p. 7), so position is not predictable from syllable count; the definite-article prefix ɨ́- attracts stress off the noun. The paper argues there is no tone contrast independent of laryngealization, i.e. no tonal system beyond stress (against Casad n.d.).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift under the stress-attracting definite article prefix; the data are words in isolation only, mono- and disyllables (longer words excluded), two speakers.
new_statements.identity_note: Jáuregui 2025 (not opened) describes Tereseño (Santa Teresa) Cora, a different Cora variety from El Nayar Cora elna1235 (the prior pass's maps it to sant1424; unverified). audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (antepenult default in 3+ syllables / initial in disyllables, with lexically marked exceptions; not in the strict set), with a caution note that Casad 1984 and Kim & Valdovinos 2014 treat stress as lexical with tone/laryngealization interactions — 'lexical' or 'conflict' if the catalog requires the modern description to govern.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote: verified verbatim in the now-held Preuss 1912 text at the cited pages. Source quality: the classification 'fixed-strict, dominant, antepenult' rests on a database pattern (StressTyp -> Gordon 2002) whose cited source (Casad 1984, held and read) gives no positional rule, backed up by a 1912 transcription-convention note that itself hedges ('sehr häufig', acute-marked exceptions, double-peaked words, fluctuating accent). Every later description of the same Jesús María variety points away from an exceptionless rule: Casad 1984 (phonemic tone partly independent of stress, primary+secondary stress, mobile-stress stems), and the instrumental pilot Kim & Valdovinos 2014 (downloaded now), which assumes lexical stress, finds initial and final stress split roughly evenly across 117 monomorphemic disyllables from two speakers (22/50 and 37/67 final), and reports a stress-attracting prefix. sources.quote: Instrumental pilot study of the same Jesús María (Mariteco) variety Preuss described. Treats Cora as having 'lexical stress' (following Casad n.d.); 'Disyllables introduce the dimension of stress to the analysis. Initial stress and final stress are both found. Cues include a high pitch prominence on the stressed syllable and devoicing of final unstressed vowels'. Counts for monomorphemic disyllables in isolation: younger speaker 28 initial-stressed vs 22 final-stressed (of 50); older speaker 30 initial vs 37 final (of 67). The definite prefix ɨ- attracts stress off the noun. No tonal contrast
